title: Fatal police shootings in Nunavik shattered trust. Can these new intervention teams help?
summary: Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) in Kuujjuaq is pairing intervention workers with officers in an effort to reduce police involvement, arrests and use of force. It comes on the heels of years…

blocks.text: The sun is nearly set by the time Ariane Richard starts her shift in Kuujjuaq, a village in northern Quebec.
And on an evening in early November, her back seat is full — with a police officer, a new intervention worker in training and a CBC News team, in tow.
After six years working in the North as an intervention worker, Richard says she's seen a lot.
"A lot of stuff you're not necessarily ready to see," she said.
But her newest role is a bit different.

For the past year, she's co-ordinated Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) and led the unit in Kuujjuaq — pairing intervention workers with officers in an effort to reduce police involvement, arrests and use of force.

Established in the northern Quebec communities of Puvirnituq, Kuujjuaq and most recently Salluit, the Inuit-led organization says the team is meant to address pressing issues: suicide prevention, intimate partner violence, mental health crises and at-risk children.
The unit takes on interventions that require time, sensitivity and follow-ups.
The team was first established in the region in 2019.
Could this intervention team help villages trust police in northern Quebec?
It expanded over the last couple of years in the shadow of eroding trust between Inuit and the Nunavik Police Service (NPS) — compounded by several high-profile police-involved shootings.

In 2024, communities across the province took part in marches to denounce police brutality in the region after police fatally shot 26-year-old Joshua Papigatuk and injured his twin brother, Garnet, in an incident that made headlines across the province.
Not long after, the family of Mark R. Annanack, who died in Kangiqsualujjuaq, Que., following a fatal police shooting, co-signed a letter calling for changes within the NPS.

blocks.text: This month, Annanack's father and Papigatuk's surviving twin brother, Garnet, issued a statement to members of the National Assembly, ministers and Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Chief of the Nunavik Police Service, Jean-François Bernier, says public trust is "coming back slowly," but that there's no doubt people ask questions following a fatal intervention. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)
The families are demanding immediate investments for an overhaul of local judicial and policing services.
"Inuit are dying and our dignity suffers," read the release, issued on a Facebook page titled "Justice for Inuit," just days ahead of the two-year anniversary of Joshua Papigatuk's death, on Nov. 4.
On Tuesday, the province's Crown prosecutor's office announced that charges would not be laid against the officers who shot and killed Joshua.
'MIT should be in every village'

Having partnerships with units like the MIT helps build trust between police and the community, says Capt. Mélanie Panneton, in charge of the southeast division for the NPS, who has worked in Nunavik for the past 11 years.
Capt. Mélanie Panneton is in charge of the southeast division for the Nunavik Police Service. She says the MIT can help build trust. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"It helps us focus on another side of policing," she said, sitting in Kuujjuaq's police headquarters, located in the centre of town.
"It's always a learning opportunity," she said. "It's beneficial to put more [of] the focus on de-escalation."
Caroline Simard, the director of youth protection for the Ungava coast, stands by the MIT approach, noting it responds to situations that aren't necessarily a policing matter.
Caroline Simard, the director of youth protection for the Ungava coast, says she sees results in how the unit builds trust with families. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
According to her, "MIT should be in every village, because it's the best way to intervene."
"It's less stressful for family to see MIT coming, just Saqijuq, than [the Department of Youth Protection]," she said.
"There's the image that we're going to take children and send them down south and then family won't ever see their children again."

blocks.text: Bringing 'softness' and fairy wings
Nunavik police officer Const. Tommy Bertrand Dell'Accio is opening his mind to a new way of doing things.
Here he was, in the backseat of Saqijuq's MIT vehicle earlier this month, holding pink sparkly fairy wings and a matching wand.
The day earlier, he says he wore the accessories after a special request from a young girl the team was assisting.

Nunavik Police officer, Const. Tommy Bertrand Dell'Accio, seen here with Sophie Bergeron, a trainee on the intervention team, held sparkly fairy wings and a matching wand at the request of a young girl the team assisted in November. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"And now she's actually asking for me to put it back again," he said smiling, during a ride-along with CBC News, on his way to meeting the girl for a second consecutive day.
The streets were dark as the team hurried to help transfer the child to a group home in the northern community, located along Quebec's Ungava Bay.
"I told you I had the wand," said Bertrand Dell'Accio, greeting her alongside Richard and the team's newest trainee, Sophie Bergeron.
He handed the girl a sparkly accessory as a gift and followed her up the group home's steps.
Later, back in the car, he noted despite his being on shift — and in uniform — his role that night was meant as a support.

blocks.text: "To show the population as well that police officer[s] are not just here to arrest people, but they're here to get involved," he said.
The MIT — when not on call — is focused on prevention and building connections by participating in local events, like karaoke, volleyball or trick-or-treating, says Richard.
Ariane Richard drove the mobile unit's car one evening in November. The unit takes on interventions that require time, sensitivity and follow-ups. (CBC)
"My goal and our goal … is really to bring a little bit of softness and joy even when it's a rough time," she said.
"There's a way to bring … happiness in any of our interventions, and that's really the goal of it."
Trust in Nunavik police was at 'its lowest,' says chief
Confidence in police has historically been lower amongst Indigenous people in Canada, as outlined in a number of Statistics Canada reports.
In the 2020 general social survey, 22 per cent of Indigenous people reported having little or no confidence in the police.
When Nunavik Police Chief Jean-François Bernier first began in the role in 2025, he says confidence in the police was at "its lowest."
"I truly understand why," said Bernier. "People need answers. They need to be closer to their police force. The police force need[s] to be more transparent."
In 2025, CBC reported that the rate of fatal shootings by police officers was roughly 73 times higher in Nunavik than the Quebec average, according to the provincial police watchdog.
Since last year, Bernier says, public trust is "coming back slowly." But he says there's no doubt people ask questions following a fatal intervention.
Nunavik Police Chief Jean-François Bernier says part of his approach to leading the department involves being on the ground and accessible. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)
Even when the Crown prosecutor determines that police acted lawfully, Bernier calls it a "lose-lose situation," that leaves families, communities — and the police service — with deep wounds.
"Because I don't know any police officers who get up in the morning and say, 'Oh, I hope I'll be involved in this serious incident and I'm going to fight for my life today,'" he said.
"It doesn't work that way."
Part of Bernier's approach to leading the department involves being on the ground and accessible, he says, and answering hard questions.

By the end of this year, he noted he will open a new position within his executive office for an Inuk advisor that will report to him. The person's mandate will be to challenge the decisions of the police service.
Rebuilding trust, Bernier says, will take time.
"Once I get the full confidence of the public, and I will," he said. "We're never going to lose the confidence again."
Problems to continue if justice is out of Inuit hands, says elder
But Charlie Watt, an Inuk elder and former Canadian senator, says he's heard that same message many times over his lifetime.
He was one of the negotiators for the 1974 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.
The agreement was Canada's first modern Indigenous land claims treaty, and signalled a new era for Nunavimmiut to gain more self-governance, including in policing.
Charlie Watt says he is thinking about creating a specialized group of Inuit to start tackling the justice issues. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
At one point, Watt pushed for the idea of setting up the police force under Inuit control. To this day, however, he says Inuit life continues to be handled by "the outside."
"We don't have our self government in place," he said. "That's our biggest enemy at the moment."
Sitting in his living room, overlooking the Kuujjuaq River, 82-year-old Watt is surrounded by mementos from his life in politics, and photos of family growing up on the other side of the river.
The modern community of Kuujjuaq, now the largest in Nunavik, completely changed over the course of Watt's lifetime.
Kuujjuaq, located along the Ungava Bay, is the largest northern village in the region of Nunavik. (Rachel Watts/CBC)
Reflecting on justice and policing systems in his region, his perspective is that the relationship between police and Inuit never used to be this bad.
"They have [a] tendency to shoot before they open their mouth," he said, pointing to the fact that some officers get training in western Canada, through the RCMP.
"You have to train them where they [are] going to do the work."
He says Inuit also have to take on more responsibility, when it comes to policing their communities.
He is thinking about leveraging his experience to help jumpstart a specialized group of Inuit to start tackling justice issues.
When it comes to long-term solutions to systemic problems, the elder says: "They can only come from the Inuit."
